11:01 SGT quoteInvesting
for gap ups & power earning candles:
Venu @Venu_7_ · 10 Aug 2026, 05:17 SGT
Most new investors & traders see a stock gap up huge on earnings and think: “I missed it.”

that one thought costs them the biggest winners of every cycle.

Let’s talk about the Power Earnings Gap (PEG) candle.

when a stock gaps up on strong earnings, most investors & traders think: "too extended. i missed it. this is the top."

that's exactly backwards.

a PEG candle is the START of a new uptrend - not the end.

but here's the part most people miss - the BASE matters.

we are not buying a stock that's already up 1000% from its base. we are buying the breakout of a Stage 1 base, powered by strong earnings. the stock isn't extended - it's entering a new phase of its uptrend.

why does it work?

institutions can't build a full position in one day. when earnings confirm their thesis, they add on strength for weeks, sometimes months. that gap-up candle is their footprint, not their exit.

what makes a valid PEG:
- stock breaks out of a Stage 1 base on strong earnings
- the gap holds - no immediate fill
- volume is massively above average
- clear institutional accumulation

this signals a character change in the stock. best example $PLTR

how to trade it:
- the LOW of the PEG candle defines your risk
- as long as the gap holds, the trend is intact
- best entries: near the PEG low, or the first controlled pullback into the 9/21-day EMA zone
- no chasing needed - patience gets you the spot

real example: $TER printed a clean PEG on July 30, 2025 - right out of its base. entry near the PEG low, and the candle itself acted as support. it ran 45% into the next earnings - then printed ANOTHER PEG and delivered 53% more. same playbook, twice.

gap-up candles create fear for most investors. institutions do the opposite - they add on strength when earnings confirm.

as William O'Neil said: "what looks cheap often goes lower. what looks expensive often goes higher."

10:56 SGTInvesting
Before you rush to buy a stock that's down 15-20% after earnings, understand one important rule: The 3-Day Rule!

What is the 3-Day Rule, and why does it matter? Let me explain.

When a stock gaps down sharply after earnings or bad news, wait at least 3 trading days before considering buying.

Why? Large institutions managing millions of shares may need several sessions to reduce their positions. The initial gap down might be just the beginning of the selling pressure.

Day 1: An initial bounce could be driven by short covering and aggressive dip buyers rather than sustained institutional demand.

Days 2 and 3: Selling pressure may continue, and the stock could make new lows as investors reassess the news.

After Day 3: Look for signs that selling pressure is fading and price is beginning to stabilize.

Before buying, check:
- Selling volume is shrinking
- Price is holding above the recent low
- You understand why the stock dropped
- The fundamental thesis remains intact

Remember, three days don't guarantee a bottom. Some stocks need several weeks or even months to build a proper base before beginning another sustained uptrend.

If the business is fundamentally broken, the stock isn't necessarily on sale. It may simply be getting repriced.

The market doesn't reward you for catching the exact bottom. Let the selling pressure fade, let the stock build a base, and let the trend confirm itself.

Missing the bottom is far better than getting caught in a downtrend

05:13 SGTInvesting
Demand is becoming a bigger driver of US inflation:

Demand-driven components contributed +1.2 percentage points to the +3.4% YoY increase in PCE inflation in August, the largest contribution since September 2023.

At the same time, supply-driven factors added +1.0 percentage point, while ambiguous factors accounted for another +1.2 percentage points.

This contrasts with the post-pandemic inflation surge, when supply disruptions were the main driver.

In 2022, supply-driven components contributed an average of +3.1 percentage points per month to headline PCE inflation, compared with +2.6 percentage points per month from demand-driven factors.

This is a key distinction for Fed policy, as rising interest rates can slow demand, while their impact on supply-side pressures is limited.

The composition of US inflation is shifting.

“I know what I should do, but I just can't do it.”

How many times have you said this?
Probably not more than me. 🤔 😄 Every trader experiences this.

Knowing what to do and actually doing it are two very different things.

@Andrew_Menaker explains why 👇
Andrew Menaker PhD @Andrew_Menaker · 29 Oct 2026, 00:08 SGT
The Deeper Reasons Why You Do What You Do:
(very long...do you have the patience to read it?)

In 1996 I sat with a bank teller a few hours after she’d had a gun pointed at her face. She wasn’t thinking about the robber anymore. She was thinking about her father, who used to raise his voice the same way the robber had.

Nothing about her rational, adult mind believed her father was in that bank. Her nervous system disagreed, and her nervous system doesn’t take votes from the rational mind. It just fires.

I spent years doing that kind of work, sitting with people in the minutes and days after something had overwhelmed their capacity to stay regulated. Many bank robberies, over a hundred of them for one institution alone.

A high profile incident at a naval airbase (also early in my career), where I had no time to consult theory and had to learn on the spot what happens to a human being when the ground disappears from under them.

Special forces operators, who taught me something I now consider the single most important sentence in performance psychology:

You do not rise to the level of your intentions, you fall to the level of your conditioning.

I didn’t walk into trading thinking any of that would apply. It applies completely.

A trader staring at an account that’s forty minutes underwater is not having a bad trading day. Often they are having a nervous system event, and the market on the screen is not the only market they’re trading.

There’s a second market running at the same time, built from every threat response, every old fear, every piece of conditioning they’ve ever absorbed.

I call it the Inner Market.

You don’t see the external market as it is. You see it as you are. And when those two markets disagree, the Inner Market usually wins, because it was installed first and it was installed harder.

In my 1:1 coaching work I've learned I\tt can be helpful to imagine two systems running inside you at all times.

One is conscious, slow, and can hold roughly one problem at a time. It’s the part of you narrating this sentence.

The other runs everything else, your heart rate, your balance, the tightness in your chest right before you hit sell a half second too late.

That second system doesn’t check in with you first. It’s efficient precisely because it skips that step, which is also exactly why it’s so hard to argue with once it’s running a pattern you no longer want.

This is why post -it notes, promises made to oneself, the great trading psychology book you just read......is forgotten or ignored so easily.

You do not rise to the level of your intentions, you fall to the level of your conditioning.

This is why willpower is such a poor tool for changing trading behavior.

You can decide with total sincerity, the night before, that tomorrow you will size correctly and wait for your setup. And you can still watch yourself chase a move by 9:42 the next morning.

That’s not weak character. That’s architecture. A small, effortful, easily depleted system trying to override a fast automatic one that’s had years of repetition behind it. It’s an unfair fight, and pretending it’s a fair one is where most discretionary traders lose the most money.

Where the Programming Actually Gets Written

Most of what’s driving that automatic system was installed early, often before you had the verbal capacity to argue with it. “I’m not enough.” “It’s dangerous to want something.” “If I get comfortable, it gets taken away.”

And staying with the familiar, even if it costs you, is the nervous system doing its job - new territory gets flagged as unfamiliar, and it carries a unique unease under the surface...this is why so many traders give back the profits made over the past 3 weeks.

Back to the early devlopment:
A child doesn’t get to reason through a painful, new, or unfamiliar experience and file it correctly. There’s no internal editor yet capable of saying, wait, is this actually true?

So it gets absorbed as fact, and it gets built into the architecture of a brain that is, at that age, unusually plastic and unusually literal.

That matters for you as a trader because the belief didn’t arrive with a label on it that says “childhood material, does not apply to markets.”

It just shows up as the flinch before you take profit too early, or the freeze right when a position needs managing, or the certainty that you personally are the kind of person who blows up good accounts.

The nervous system doesn’t file these things by category. It files them by intensity.

Neurons That Fire Together, Wire Together

This is a long post...and if you got this far...if there's one key idea to keep from all of this, keep this one. It’s called Hebbian learning, and it’s about as solid as anything gets in neuroscience.

When two neurons fire together repeatedly, the connection between them physically strengthens.

And that cuts in your favor as much as against you. If a pattern got built through repetition, it can be rebuilt through repetition.

There’s no rare gift required and no secret shortcut that skips the reps.

The brain keeps reorganizing itself across the entire lifespan. Neuroscientists Antonio Damasio and Lisa Feldman Barrett have both, from different angles, made the case that the brain isn’t a passive recorder of the world at all. It’s a prediction machine, constantly forecasting what should happen next based on what it already believes, then filtering incoming reality through that forecast.

Which means two traders can watch the same price action and have two completely different nervous systems tell them two completely different stories about what it means and what to do.

The Gap Between the Event and the Reaction

There’s a hard line between two kinds of memory. Explicit memory is what you’d testify to, the facts, the dates, the words someone used. Implicit memory is procedural and emotional, mostly out of reach of direct recall, which is why a setup that merely resembles an old losing trade can spike your heart rate with no conscious memory of the original loss attached to it at all.

That’s the mismatch behind a sentence I hear constantly in this work:

“I know what I should do, but just can't do it"

You’re not being irrational. You’re running an implicit prediction your conscious mind never got invited to review.

Real change starts in the half second between the trigger and the automatic reaction. Widen that gap even slightly, notice the trigger, notice the thought, the bodily sensation, the feeling, and you get leverage over a pattern that used to run you completely.

Skip that gap and you get the same result you’ve always gotten.

This is also part of reason for keeping a written trading journal that goes past P&L, one that tracks the internal state around the trade, not just the entries and exits.

Externalizing a thought onto paper drags implicit material into a system that’s actually capable of evaluating it.

That’s not a soft, optional add-on to trading psychology. It’s the mechanism.

Identity Beats Strategy, Every Time
And It's why most attempts at fixing trading behavior don’t work.

A trader tries to bolt a new rule onto an old identity.

Three weeks of discipline, then a snap back to the exact old pattern. If somewhere underneath the strategy you still believe “I’m not a disciplined trader,” or "I am not enough", the nervous system will keep steering you back toward evidence that confirms it, because confirming existing beliefs is close to the entire job of a predictive brain.

Change the underlying belief about who you are as a trader, and the behavior stops being a daily fight you have to win. It starts matching who you’ve actually decided you are.

State Comes Before Insight

The brain is not equally open to new input at every moment. A dysregulated nervous system, flooded, hypervigilant, defended, is not in a state where new learning lands.

This is precisely what I saw over and over in early in my career....crisis work, in the bank robbery debriefs, the military threat assessment work, in the sessions with people who’d just been through something that overwhelmed their capacity to stay regulated.

You cannot install a new belief into a system that’s actively defending itself. States of genuine calm, focused attention, reduced defensiveness, make the mind receptive in a way a flooded, threat state simply can’t match.

Emotion is what encodes a belief, not repetition on its own. A belief absorbed during real fear, shame, or humiliation gets burned in fast, sometimes in a single exposure, because emotional arousal amplifies memory consolidation.

This is why one brutal drawdown can outweigh months of clean, boring, profitable trading in a trader’s actual sense of who they are. And it’s why a new belief has to be paired with real felt conviction to have any chance of competing with the old one.

Flat repetition doesn’t stand a chance against a belief that arrived soaked in feeling.

It's also why affirmations don't work so well for traders.

Evidence Does the Work Affirmation Can’t

Telling yourself “I’m a disciplined trader” while your last six months of trade logs say otherwise doesn’t just fail to help. It can backfire, because the nervous system checks new statements against the evidence bank it’s already built and flags anything that doesn’t match.

What actually works - what I see in my coaching practice and it shows up consistently in the clinical literature - is building an evidence case. Naming the belief you want installed, then going back through your own trading history and finding the specific, concrete moments that already support it.

Ten real instances where you did hold the position, did size correctly, did wait for your setup, do more rewiring work than a hundred repetitions of a sentence you don’t yet believe.

This Takes Longer Than You Want It To

Structurally embedded change takes at least several weeks (sometimes longer) of consistent practice, not a weekend and not a single insight, however good that insight felt in the moment.

That’s frustrating to hear if you’re carrying a pattern that’s many years old and hoping this week is the one where it finally resolves. But it was built through thousands of small repeated moments spread across years, and undoing it runs on the same physical rules.

The genuinely useful part of that fact is that the timeline is knowable. It isn’t an indefinite wait for a feeling to fade on its own. It’s a process with a method and a reasonably predictable arc, provided you actually do the work instead of just understanding it.

This is where skilled 1:1 coaching comes in.

You’ve spent hundreds of hours training your read on price. Almost nobody spend seven a fraction of that time training the nervous system that is actually reading the price.

The disconnect between oil stocks and the broader market has rarely been wider:

The 6-month correlation between the S&P 500 Energy Sector and the S&P 500 is down to -0.38, near its lowest on record.

This marks a sharp reversal from a positive correlation of +0.74 observed in June 2025.

In the last week of September, this figure fell as low as -0.45, the lowest reading in data going back to the 1980s.

The only other time since the late 1980s when the correlation between these two indices turned negative was in 2000 and 2001, during the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

This all comes as the S&P 500 Energy Sector has rallied +23.1% over the last 6 months, significantly outperforming the S&P 500’s gain of +7.1%.

Energy stocks are having a historic year amid the Iran War.

Furthermore, consumers reported improved perceptions of the job market and business conditions.

Consumer confidence remains highly volatile.

It's officially Fed day.

We expect a "hawkish pause" today.

The Fed will hold interest rates unchanged but lay the groundwork for a December rate hike, bringing total rate hikes in 2026 to +50 basis points.

Why?

Because the US economy is now facing both supply-side and rising demand-side inflationary pressures, while the labor market continues to weaken beneath the surface.

This puts the Fed in an increasingly difficult position: Inflation is demanding tighter monetary policy, while underlying labor market weakness is calling for the opposite.

We expect the Fed to prioritize inflation today, keeping the door open for further tightening in December.

The 20-day correlation between the 10Y Note Yield and the Nasdaq 100 is up to +0.51, its highest since the March pullback.

The Treasury market is regaining its role as a defensive trade.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Robinhood $HOOD reported Q3 2026 revenue of $1.4B, up 12% YoY but slightly below the $1.42B estimate, while EPS of $0.51 missed expectations of $0.56, including a $0.07 per-share unrealized investment loss primarily tied to Robinhood Ventures Fund I. Net income declined 14% to $476M, while adjusted EBITDA increased 9% to $808M. Transaction-based revenue grew 19% to $867M, partially offset by a 9% decline in net interest revenue to $415M. Meanwhile, total platform assets climbed 19% to $396B, funded customers increased 7% to 28.7M, and Gold subscribers surged 34% to 5.2M, supported by $15.7B in net deposits. Robinhood now has 14 business lines generating over $100M in annualized revenue, with Rothera surpassing $100M in its first full quarter. CEO Vlad Tenev emphasized that customers are entrusting more assets to the platform as Robinhood expands its financial services ecosystem, although earnings growth continues to lag revenue growth.

2. SoFi $SOFI delivered a strong Q3 2026, with revenue surging 44% YoY to $1.4B, while adjusted EPS increased 64% to $0.18 and adjusted EBITDA jumped 70% to $469.8M, highlighting accelerating growth and improving profitability. Total members climbed 35% YoY to 17.1M, reflecting continued expansion across SoFi's financial services ecosystem. Looking ahead, the company issued bullish FY2027 guidance, projecting $6.4B in revenue versus $6B expected, EPS of $0.90 versus $0.82 expected, adjusted EBITDA of $2.24B, and net income of $1.28B. CEO Anthony Noto emphasized that SoFi is attracting more members, increasing the number of products used per customer, and generating more revenue per product, reinforcing management's confidence in the company's long-term growth and profitability trajectory.

3. Chinese technology giants Alibaba $BABA, Tencent, and ByteDance are reportedly seeking long-term memory supply agreements with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, according to Korean media, as demand for AI data center infrastructure continues to accelerate. While traditional memory supply contracts typically span 3–5 years, some Chinese cloud service providers are now requesting 10-year agreements extending through 2035 to secure access to critical DDR5 and LPDDR5 memory. The unusually long contract terms highlight growing concerns over future memory availability as hyperscalers expand AI computing capacity and compete for limited supply. The development could provide Samsung and SK Hynix with greater long-term revenue visibility and reinforces the structural demand outlook for the broader memory industry, including Micron $MU.

4. Meta $META has reportedly upsized its Class A common stock offering to $25B from $22.5B, pricing the shares at $625 each as the company raises additional capital to support its massive AI infrastructure expansion. Notably, NVIDIA $NVDA is investing $3B in the offering, while AMD $AMD is committing another $1B, giving two of Meta's major AI chip suppliers direct equity exposure to one of their largest customers. The expanded offering highlights Meta's increasingly aggressive capital-raising strategy as it prepares to spend $135B–$145B on capital expenditures in 2026. The participation of NVIDIA and AMD also underscores the growing financial interconnectedness of the AI ecosystem, with semiconductor suppliers investing directly in the hyperscalers purchasing their hardware.

5. Qualcomm $QCOM and Anduril are teaming up to launch BlueChip, a new venture focused on manufacturing rugged, waterproof, American-made laptops for the U.S. military, government agencies, law enforcement, and first responders, according to the Wall Street Journal. The devices will be assembled at Anduril's Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio and powered by Qualcomm Snapdragon X processors manufactured by TSMC in Arizona. Anduril founder Palmer Luckey said approximately 90% of the planned components already come from the U.S. and allied countries, with the long-term goal of producing the entire laptop domestically, including displays and other components currently sourced overseas. The initiative prioritizes secure computing, fully traceable supply chains, and reduced dependence on foreign manufacturing for national-security applications. The first laptops are expected in 2027, with pricing estimated at roughly 20% above conventional high-end PCs.

6. President Donald Trump made two major statements, reiterating his administration's decision to replace the terms “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” with “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in official executive-branch communications, following a September executive order. Separately, Trump suggested that Venezuela could eventually become the 51st U.S. state, floating the possibility of replacing its presidency with a governorship during remarks in Corpus Christi, Texas. Trump also celebrated the U.S. military intervention in Venezuela and its subsequent oil agreement, describing the operation as a historic victory and highlighting expanded American access to Venezuelan oil reserves.

7. Tesla $TSLA rallied approximately 4% on Tuesday to $407.46, extending Monday's 5.2% gain as shares broke above key technical resistance levels. The rally was primarily fueled by Barclays upgrading Tesla to Overweight and raising its price target to $450 from $370, citing improving automotive demand, accelerating energy storage growth, and a potential merger with SpaceX $SPCX that could create a premium for Tesla shareholders. Meanwhile, Tesla's robotaxi expansion continues to gain momentum, with its Texas fleet reportedly exceeding 1,050 vehicles, Cybercabs outnumbering Model Ys, and additional service areas planned, including Dallas. Investors are also responding to improving FSD adoption, strong demand for energy storage from AI data centers, and signs of stabilization in Tesla's core automotive business.

8. Brazil's stock market experienced an extraordinary selloff on October 26, with the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF $EWZ plunging 19.8% in a single session, representing an estimated 8.4-standard-deviation move based on its historical daily volatility. Over the past 20 years, EWZ has averaged a daily return of approximately 0.04%, with a standard deviation of 2.36%, making Monday's decline an extreme statistical outlier. Under a theoretical normal distribution, a move of this magnitude would have an exceptionally small probability, illustrating just how unusual the selloff was relative to historical volatility. However, actual financial markets exhibit fat-tailed return distributions, meaning extreme declines occur more frequently than conventional statistical models predict. The plunge highlights the severity of the selling pressure in Brazilian equities and the risks associated with sudden market shocks.

9. Alphabet's $GOOGL Waymo is expanding its fully autonomous ride-hailing service by nearly 250 square miles across five existing U.S. markets over the next week, further accelerating its commercial robotaxi rollout. In Los Angeles, Waymo is extending service along the coast into the South Bay, including Torrance, while San Diego coverage will expand north to La Jolla, connecting riders to UC San Diego, the VA, and University Town Center. In Nashville, the company is expanding south to include Nashville Zoo, while Orlando will see its eastern service area nearly double alongside improved downtown coverage. The San Francisco Bay Area will also gain additional southern coverage, including a connection to Berryessa BART Station. The expansion increases Waymo's geographic reach and the number of destinations accessible to existing riders, rather than representing launches in five new cities, as Alphabet continues scaling its autonomous transportation network.

10. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 2.4M contracts, $TSLA with 2.3M contracts, $AAPL with 1.2M contracts, $SOFI with 944K contracts, $SPCX with 852K contracts, $AMZN with 833K contracts, $MU with 716K contracts, $META with 709K contracts, $GOOGL with 529K contracts, and $AMD with 529K contracts.

11. Amazon $AMZN is reportedly working to reduce its reliance on Anthropic's AI models as the cost of operating Alexa+ continues to climb, according to Business Insider. Internal projections estimated that Alexa+ cloud computing expenses could reach approximately $1.7B in 2026, nearly triple the prior year's costs, prompting Amazon to explore routing more AI requests through its own lower-cost models and infrastructure. The company also considered delaying or scaling back Moonraker, its advanced AI agent initiative, which was projected to require more than $100M in GPU spending this year. The developments highlight the growing pressure on major technology companies to improve AI inference economics, reduce dependence on third-party model providers, and balance increasingly expensive AI capabilities with sustainable profitability.

12. U.S. stock market breadth is improving significantly, with the S&P 500 Equal-Weight Index outperforming the traditional market-cap-weighted S&P 500 by 4.0 percentage points in October, putting it on track for its second-strongest monthly relative performance since April 2009. The equal-weight index has gained 4.3% this month, compared with just 0.3% for the S&P 500, marking a sharp reversal from September, when equal-weight stocks underperformed by 4.7 percentage points, their worst relative month since March 2020. For comparison, the equal-weight index outperformed by 4.2 percentage points in April. Year-to-date, the Equal-Weight Index is up 13.4% versus 12.1% for the S&P 500, suggesting market leadership is broadening beyond the largest technology and AI companies as more sectors and individual stocks participate in the rally.

05:11 SGTInvesting
Is China hiding its true exposure to US Treasuries?

China’s Treasury holdings fell -$27 billion in August, to $591 billion, their lowest level since August 2008.

At the same time, Canada’s holdings of US Treasuries jumped +$38 billion in August, to $465 billion, their 3rd-highest on record.

Since the beginning of 2019, Canada’s holdings have surged +$369 billion, or +384%, while China’s have declined -$534 billion, or -48%.

This divergence may partly reflect China moving its US securities to foreign custodians, making its actual exposure to American debt appear smaller and creating the impression of faster financial decoupling from the US Dollar.

Meanwhile, Belgium and Luxembourg, widely believed to hold some Chinese Treasury assets through custodial accounts, increased their Treasury holdings by +$20 billion and +$6 billion in August, to all-time highs of $491 billion and $448 billion, respectively.

China’s diversification away from the US Dollar may be slower than it appears.

Blackstone’s Jon Gray says neoclouds that can get to the other side will find compute pricing up 50% and legacy chips worth more than people thought, and the market is confusing deliverability with demand

“I think what we’re seeing in the market is a little bit of a conflation between deliverability of compute and demand for compute. And at our companies, as an example, we’ve seen a 20-fold increase in spend on models over the last 12 months. It’s pretty extraordinary."

"We have a joint venture with Anthropic to deploy these models. The company’s called Ode, and it can’t keep up with the business that’s coming in the door. So we’re seeing demand really growing for compute."

"And at the same time, the constraint, of course, is delivering that supply. And that’s hard because of amassing capital, data centers, power, chips, all of that."

"And so for the neoclouds, if they can get to the other side, the pricing of compute’s up 50%. Their legacy chips are worth much more than people thought. Their data centers are leased below market."

"Their challenge is, do they have the capital, the debt and equity and the quantum that’s needed to deliver?"

"I think some of these companies have very talented CEOs. CoreWeave’s a good example of this. They’ll find a way through it, but that’s the challenge they face. The underlying business is actually quite strong.”

same bar for PMs shipping agent-written PRDs. if you can't defend why X over Y at the whiteboard, you didn't write it
Mitchell Hashimoto @mitchellh · 16 Sep 2026, 23:44 SGT
The "whiteboard defense:" I should be able to pull you aside at any moment and ask you to explain any customer-facing system you've shipped. You should be able to clearly explain how it works and defend the decisions you made. This is my benchmark for responsible AI usage.

I don't expect line-level familiarity with the code. I don't care if you remember the exact function name or implementation detail. You may not even know it. I don't care.

But if I ask "why did you do X instead of Y?", "what happens if this actor behaves maliciously?", "what data structure did you use here and why?", or "where does this fail?" you should be able to answer confidently.

For PoCs, demos, experiments, whatever: I don't care. Generate 100% of it and understand none of it. Speed over quality every time in those specific scenarios.

But if you're shipping customer-facing work, you can't be shipping things you don't understand at a high level.

BREAKING: Brazil's -19.8% stock market crash on Monday was one of the rarest market events in the last two decades, according to our analysis.

Brazil's EWZ ETF plunged -19.8% on October 26th, marking an 8.4 standard deviation move.

For context, the ETF's average daily move over the last 20 years has been just +0.04%, with a standard deviation of 2.36%.

Under a normal distribution, the probability of a decline this extreme is approximately 1 in 58 quadrillion.

In other words, this event should be virtually impossible under conventional statistical models.

What just happened in Brazil was *almost* impossible.

By comparison, pension and retirement funds own 8% of the market, while hedge funds own just 1%.

Household demand for stocks is stronger than ever.

21:59 SGTInvesting
When to buy the dip?

Buy dips in uptrends. Avoid them in downtrends.

In a Stage 2 uptrend, price makes higher highs and higher lows above a rising 200-day SMA. Pullbacks on lighter volume toward rising moving averages often attract buyers, as those averages can act as support.

In a Stage 4 downtrend, the opposite happens. Price makes lower highs and lower lows, while rallies toward declining moving averages often face selling pressure. What once acted as support can become resistance.

A stock trading below a declining 200-day SMA might look cheap, but cheap can always get cheaper.

Before buying a dip, look for:
- Price above a rising 200-day SMA
- Higher highs and higher lows
- Pullbacks on lighter volume toward rising moving averages
- Signs of buyers stepping in at support

The goal isn’t to buy a stock simply because it’s fallen. It’s to buy strength during temporary weakness.

Buy the pullback in an uptrend, not the breakdown in a downtrend.

US stocks tend to rally following Midterm elections:

The S&P 500 has returned +17.2% on average in the year following Midterm elections since 1950, the strongest return of any year in the Presidential cycle.

The index has finished higher in 17 of the 19 post-Midterm years during this period.

This is also nearly quadruple the +4.6% average return recorded during midterm years, when the index finished higher in 11 of 19 years.

By comparison, the S&P 500 has returned +8.1% on average in Year 4 of the Presidential cycle, or during Presidential election years, ending higher in 16 of 19 years.

In Q4 of Midterm years, the S&P 500 has delivered an average return of +6.6% since 1950, the strongest quarterly return of the Presidential cycle.

History suggests US equities will extend their rally after Midterm elections.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. SpaceX $SPCX has signed a binding commitment letter with an Apollo Global Management-managed entity for a massive $40B GPU financing arrangement to support its expanding AI data center infrastructure. Under the proposed agreement, Apollo's entity would purchase GPU pods and related data center equipment and lease them to SpaceX, with approximately $40B in aggregate principal payments spread across lease terms of 5 to 5.25 years. The transaction is expected to close before year-end, with GPU deliveries and lease payments beginning in the first half of 2027. Importantly, the $40B figure excludes interest and additional financing costs, with the final borrowing rate still to be determined, highlighting the enormous capital requirements behind SpaceX's AI infrastructure expansion.

2. Anthropic has reportedly filed its S-1 for a U.S. IPO, seeking to list on the Nasdaq under ticker $ANT, with Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and JPMorgan leading the offering. The filing shows explosive growth, with H1 2026 revenue surging to $16.3B from $1.16B a year earlier, including $13.1B in consumption-based revenue and $3.2B from subscriptions. Anthropic now has more than 11,900 customers spending $100K+ annually, including 1,900 spending over $1M and approximately 250 spending over $10M, while net revenue retention reached roughly 900% as of September 30. Despite the growth, Anthropic reported an $80.7B net loss, largely driven by a $72.4B noncash fair-value charge tied to convertible notes, while its operating loss narrowed to $693M. The biggest revelation is the company's enormous AI infrastructure commitments extending as far as 2045, including approximately $161B in Broadcom TPU leases, $120.5B with SpaceXAI, $114.5B with Google, $110B with Amazon, $44.9B with Microsoft, and tens of billions more with Nscale, Lambda, and AMD, alongside roughly $245B in additional agreements signed after June 30. Anthropic also disclosed $131.7B in cash and short-term investments, plans to allocate 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund, and a governance structure preserving 50.1% voting control for its founders, highlighting both the extraordinary scale of its growth and the capital intensity of the frontier AI industry.

3. Barclays upgraded Tesla $TSLA to Overweight from Equal Weight, raising its price target to $450 from $370, as analyst Dan Levy sees an increasingly attractive risk/reward profile. Levy noted that much of the recent discussion surrounding Tesla has focused on a potential merger with SpaceX $SPCX, which he believes could result in a premium for Tesla shareholders. However, his bullish thesis extends beyond a possible combination, citing improving automotive demand, strong growth in Tesla's energy business, and a sharp acceleration in Robotaxi miles driven. Barclays also highlighted FSD adoption exceeding 75% of new North American vehicle deliveries, suggesting growing monetization opportunities for Tesla's autonomous driving technology. Together, these factors underpin the firm's more constructive outlook on Tesla's long-term growth potential.

4. Microsoft $MSFT is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, representing more than 25% of its global workforce, as the company moves to restructure parts of its operations. The program reportedly covers select teams across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, and India, with eligible employees receiving severance packages in exchange for voluntarily leaving the company. Employees have until early December to decide whether to participate, with departures expected to take place by year-end. The move could represent one of Microsoft's largest workforce restructuring initiatives, although the final number of departures will depend on employee participation.

5. Samsung and SK Hynix are reportedly targeting Q2 2027 to begin mass production and shipments of 8-layer HBM4 memory for NVIDIA $NVDA, according to ZDNet Korea. The advanced memory is expected to be used in NVIDIA's next-generation Rubin Ultra rack-scale AI systems, supporting the growing memory requirements of increasingly powerful AI accelerators. While 12-layer HBM4 remains the primary focus throughout 2026, the share of 8-layer HBM4 shipments is expected to increase significantly beginning in mid-2027. The development highlights the continued expansion of the high-bandwidth memory market as Samsung and SK Hynix prepare additional capacity for NVIDIA's next generation of AI infrastructure.

6. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $TSLA with 3.4M contracts, $NVDA with 3.1M contracts, $AAPL with 1.6M contracts, $MU with 1.3M contracts, $SPCX with 1.3M contracts, $META with 979K contracts, $AMZN with 884K contracts, $NFLX with 624K contracts, $INTC with 598K contracts, and $AMD with 550K contracts.

7. Meta $META announced plans to raise approximately $35B through new equity offerings, including $22.5B in Class A common stock through forward sale agreements and $12.5B in depositary shares tied to mandatory convertible preferred stock. The company is also considering a separate $60B offering program for its new nonvoting Class C shares beginning in Q1 2027, potentially bringing its total equity financing capacity to $95B, approximately $10B more than Google's $85B equity offering earlier this year. Interestingly, NVIDIA $NVDA, AMD $AMD, and Broadcom $AVGO have expressed nonbinding interest in purchasing up to $5B of Meta shares combined, potentially giving major AI chip suppliers direct equity exposure to one of their largest customers. The proposed financing comes as Meta prepares for unprecedented AI infrastructure spending, while its new Class C share structure, introduced alongside an effective 2-for-1 stock split, would allow the company to raise additional capital without issuing new voting rights. The full $95B remains potential financing capacity rather than a completed capital raise.

8. DoorDash $DASH is reportedly in advanced negotiations to acquire Instacart $CART, with a potential agreement expected as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The discussions follow earlier reports that Instacart had attracted takeover interest from both DoorDash and Uber $UBER, although talks with Uber are reportedly no longer active. A combination would significantly expand DoorDash's presence in online grocery delivery, combining Instacart's grocery partnerships and fulfillment technology with DoorDash's restaurant delivery network and logistics infrastructure. The potential acquisition could strengthen DoorDash's competitive position across local commerce, although no final agreement has been announced and negotiations could still fall apart.

9. The 10 largest U.S. leveraged equity ETFs attracted approximately $12B in net inflows over the past month, even as their combined market capitalization declined by $20B, highlighting aggressive dip-buying despite the broader market selloff. The surge was led by the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF $SOXL, which attracted a record $9B in inflows over just two weeks, while the ProShares UltraPro QQQ $TQQQ, which provides 3x leveraged exposure to the Nasdaq 100, recorded $1.3B in inflows, its second-largest two-week intake of 2026. Over the past five months, the 10 largest leveraged equity ETFs have collectively attracted $19B, suggesting that speculative investors are continuing to increase leveraged exposure to semiconductors and technology stocks even as market volatility and downside risks remain elevated.

10. Morgan Stanley strategist Michael Wilson expects the current U.S. equity market correction to eventually give way to a rebound as several major uncertainties begin to clear, including the midterm elections, AI infrastructure financing concerns, and tightening financial conditions. Wilson sees potential near-term downside for the S&P 500 $SPX to 7,100–7,200, but maintains a year-end base-case target of 8,000, suggesting meaningful recovery potential if market conditions improve. He identified liquidity constraints as the biggest immediate risk, while arguing that a potential Federal Reserve policy pivot could provide an important catalyst for equities. Morgan Stanley also pointed to historically strong 6–12-month stock market returns following midterm elections, supporting its view that the current correction could ultimately create buying opportunities rather than mark the end of the broader market cycle.

11. UBS pushed back against concerns that CoreWeave $CRWV could face a debt spiral as credit markets tighten, arguing that the company has multiple financing alternatives to support its AI infrastructure expansion. UBS highlighted opportunities to reduce reliance on traditional debt through private credit, vendor financing, and additional equity investments, similar to CoreWeave's recent transaction with Jane Street. Following meetings with private credit executives and data center developers, UBS said it “did NOT come away with a view that capital will be scarce in 2027,” suggesting financing conditions may remain more supportive than investors fear. Separately, Cantor Fitzgerald reiterated its Overweight rating and $176 price target on CoreWeave, citing the potential for delayed-draw term loan (DDTL) credit enhancements to attract additional lenders and new financing facilities to ease concerns over the company's access to capital.

12. The United States and Canada are reportedly negotiating a potential agreement to ease tariffs on Canadian steel and automobiles, according to Reuters, citing six sources familiar with the discussions. Negotiations are focused on Section 232 tariffs, including duties of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on automobiles, with one Canadian source suggesting a deal could be reached before the November 3 midterm elections. U.S. officials are reportedly seeking additional concessions from Canada. The discussions come as President Trump has threatened to raise steel and auto tariffs to 50% beginning January 1, 2027, although he recently suggested the trade dispute could be resolved “soon.” Canadian officials described the negotiations as constructive, but no agreement has been finalized.

Today was a dead cat bounce?

Background context: Hedge funds still seem heavily underweight tech relative to consensus Q3 earnings growth. The recent unwind has flushed out crowded positioning, cut concentration and brought multiples back towards more "normal" levels across Tech/Semis.

That said...I do feel like we're getting close to the end of this unwind now especially with hyperscalers sticking to capex plans & Q3 semis earnings likely to be positive.

Microsoft 0.01x

Oracle 0.33x
CoreWeave 1.17x
The bitcoin miners turned AI hosts: 0.76x to 1.68x

Nebius borrowed ahead of a revenue ramp that’s already signed, with Microsoft and Meta behind it

Yet the market keeps lumping it in with every other NeoCloud and the Bitcoin miners.

I’ll wait patiently for earnings on Nov 12.

Anthropic's S-1 shows that revenue is speeding ahead of its compute costs.

> Revenue up ~31x in six quarters; compute costs up ~6x

> Q1 2025: compute spend was 251% of revenue.
> Q1 2026: revenue overtook compute for the first time.
> Q2 2026: compute down to 48% of revenue ($5.6B vs $11.6B).

Revenue from new model/product launches has more than offset Anthropic's rising compute costs.

Caveat:
> Bigger compute costs are coming: the SPCX deal alone is ~$3.1B/mth once fully delivered (expected Dec).
> A warning in the S-1 is that margins may compress as new capacity is expensed before revenue arrives.

amit@amitisinvesting
00:21 SGTInvesting
ANTHROPIC'S IPO DOCUMENTS ARE CALMING DOWN THE MARKETS.

None of the numbers released today are that different from what we heard last week, but now we know how much cash they have.

Anthropic has $120B in cash and is likely raising $100B on the IPO. They are then likely going to be raising another $100B in debt, $60B of it already financed by BlackStone. If you assume a 3x in ARR, which probably is low considering how much the street wants them to grow, this company should have around $300-$400B in cash. This also doesn't take into account the future ATMs they might engage in.

So, the reason AI stocks are getting some relief right now is because it seems like Anthropic will have enough cash to pay their bills, which obviously is good for $NVDA, $SPCX, $AMD, $AVGO, $MU, and many other players.

However, there are going to be 24 separate unlocks in 2027. Those are going to be days where the market has to deal with a massive amount of supply coming onto the market. The company effectively has unilateral control, not shareholders, on deciding to pause or slow down the release of models. The open-weight models continue to be a threat as more enterprises are seeing the value in owning their AI for a significantly cheaper cost. Anthropic has outlined all these risks in the S1.

Regardless on if you are buying the IPO, it seems like there is enough cash they can raise to continue paying their bills and making sure the downstream value flows into most of the semis...if the market changes their mind on that or Anthropic stalls in growth, those names get hit. But if the company keeps growing and raises cash, the money should be there to fund the semis...it's now a question on how much of a risk people want to take in actually owning the stock.
